definition: The company that launches and manages mutual fund schemes. It pools money from investors and its fund managers invest it according to each scheme's stated objective.
The Association of Mutual Funds in India, the industry body for mutual funds. It registers mutual fund distributors and issues their ARN.
A unique number issued by AMFI to a registered mutual fund distributor. You can verify a distributor's ARN on the AMFI website.
How your money is divided across asset classes such as equity, debt and gold. It is shaped by your goals, time horizon and comfort with risk, and has a large effect on long-term outcomes.
The total market value of the investments a fund or fund house manages on behalf of its investors.
A market index, such as the Nifty 50, that a fund's performance is compared against to judge how well it has done.
The steady yearly rate at which an investment would have grown from its starting value to its ending value. Best suited to single, one-time investments.
Earning returns on your past returns as well as on your original investment. The effect grows stronger the longer you stay invested.
A mutual fund that invests mainly in fixed-income instruments such as government securities, corporate bonds and money market instruments. Usually less volatile than equity, but not risk-free.

Two versions of the same scheme. A direct plan is bought straight from the fund house. A regular plan is bought through a distributor, includes distributor commission, and so has a slightly higher expense ratio.
Spreading investments across companies, sectors and asset classes so that a fall in any one of them has a smaller impact on your overall portfolio.
An equity mutual fund with a three-year lock-in. Investments may qualify for a tax deduction under Section 80C under the old tax regime.
A mutual fund that invests mainly in company shares. It aims for long-term growth and can move up and down sharply in the short term.
A fee some schemes charge if you redeem units before a set period. It is deducted from the redemption value and is disclosed in the scheme documents.
The yearly cost of running a fund, shown as a percentage of its assets. It is deducted from the fund's NAV, so returns you see are already net of it.
An account number a fund house gives you to track your holdings, transactions and statements with that fund house.
Planning investments around specific goals such as education, a home or retirement, with an amount and timeline for each, instead of picking products first.
A mutual fund that invests in a mix of asset classes, typically equity and debt, to balance growth with stability.
A passively managed fund that aims to track a market index, such as the Nifty 50, by holding the same securities in the same proportions.
A one-time identity and address verification required before investing in mutual funds. It is completed using documents such as PAN and Aadhaar.
Categories of companies by market value. Large caps are the biggest and usually most stable, small caps are the smallest and usually most volatile, and mid caps sit in between.
A fixed period during which an investment cannot be redeemed, such as the three-year lock-in on ELSS funds.
Investing a larger amount in one go, as opposed to spreading it out over time through a SIP.
The per-unit value of a mutual fund, calculated at the end of each business day. Purchases and redemptions happen at the applicable NAV.
The person you name to receive your investments in the event of your death. Keeping nominations up to date makes the transfer simpler for your family.
A government-backed, long-term retirement savings scheme regulated by the PFRDA. Contributions are invested in a mix of equity, corporate bonds and government securities.
A SEBI-regulated service where a professional manager runs a portfolio of securities held directly in your name. It has a high minimum investment and suits experienced investors.
A periodic check of your investments against your goals, looking at allocation, overlap between funds, performance and costs.
Bringing your portfolio back to its target asset allocation after market movements have shifted it, by trimming what has grown and adding to what has lagged.
Selling your mutual fund units back to the fund house. The money is paid out at the applicable NAV, less any exit load.
A SEBI-mandated label on every mutual fund that shows its risk level on a scale from Low to Very High.
The Securities and Exchange Board of India, the regulator for securities markets, mutual funds and portfolio managers in India.
A SEBI-regulated category that sits between mutual funds and PMS. It allows more flexible strategies than mutual funds and has a higher minimum investment.
Investing a fixed amount in a mutual fund at regular intervals, usually monthly. It builds discipline and spreads your purchases across market ups and downs.
A SIP where the instalment increases by a set amount or percentage each year, usually in line with growth in income.
Moving a fixed amount at regular intervals from one scheme to another within the same fund house, often from a debt fund into an equity fund.
Withdrawing a fixed amount from a mutual fund at regular intervals, often used to create a steady income in retirement.
Pure life cover that pays a fixed sum to your nominee if you die during the policy term. It has no investment component, which keeps premiums low.
Your share of a mutual fund. The number of units you receive equals the amount invested divided by the NAV.
An annualised return that accounts for the timing of each cash flow. It is the right way to measure returns on SIPs and investments made over time.
